evidence: createApp() builds new Catalogue(), new OrderService(catalogue) and new CatalogueService(catalogue): this is composition-root wiring, which belongs in infrastructure.
catalogueService.addProduct('PROD001', 'Laptop', 999.99, 5) and the similar calls seed sample fixture data through the application service. This is bootstrap setup, not domain logic.
app.post('/orders') only checks the request shape (Array.isArray(items) && items.length > 0) and then calls orderService.createOrder(items). This is transport-level validation.
app.patch('/orders/:orderId/state') calls orderService.transitionOrder(orderId, state). The rules for state transitions stay in the application or domain layer.
The try/catch blocks turn errors into res.status(400).json({ error }), which is HTTP error mapping and belongs in the transport adapter.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: src/infrastructure/app.ts does three things, and all of them belong in the infrastructure layer. First, it is the composition root: it builds the Catalogue and the application services. Second, it seeds bootstrap data with fixed sample products, which is fixture setup, not a business rule. Third, it is the HTTP transport adapter, made of Express route handlers. The handlers only read request parameters and the body, do basic input-shape checks (the items array must exist and not be empty; state must be present), hand the work to OrderService and CatalogueService, and turn the results or errors into HTTP status codes and JSON. Order state transitions, stock checks, pricing and cancellation rules are all left to the application services. Nothing in the file handles persistence for the domain or makes business decisions. Hardcoding the sample data inside createApp is a little unusual, but it is startup setup, not a misplaced business responsibility.
